title: Problem #1068: Countable Infinitely-Connected Subgraphs — Overview and Setup
content: The module docstring frames Problem #1068 (Erdős-Hajnal): does every graph with chromatic number ℵ₁ contain a countable subgraph that is infinitely connected? This is a weakening of Problem #1067 (asking for an uncountable subgraph with the same chromatic number), which was disproved by Soukup (2015) — who constructed a graph with χ = ℵ₁ where every uncountable vertex set induces only finitely vertex-connected subgraphs. Problem #1068 targets countable subgraphs specifically, which Soukup's construction leaves open. The answer may depend on set-theoretic axioms beyond ZFC. The setup imports Mathlib's SimpleGraph, Cardinal, and Set.Countable, then opens the Erdos1068 namespace.
mathContext: Problem #1068: $\forall G$ with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$, $\exists S \subseteq V(G)$ countable such that $G[S]$ is $\infty$-connected? Known: Soukup (2015) proved $\exists G$ with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ where every uncountable $S$ gives finitely-connected $G[S]$. Open: same for countable $S$. References: [ErHa66] (Erdős-Hajnal 1966), [Va99, 7.90] (Väänänen survey 1999).

title: Imports: Graph Theory and Set Theory
content: Imports Mathlib's `SimpleGraph` for graph infrastructure, `Cardinal` for uncountable cardinals ($\aleph_1$), and `Set.Countable` for the countability predicate. This combination bridges finite combinatorics (graph coloring, paths) with infinite set theory (uncountable cardinals, countable sets).
mathContext: Uses $\texttt{SimpleGraph}$ for undirected graphs, $\texttt{Cardinal}$ for $\aleph_0, \aleph_1$, and $\texttt{Set.Countable}$ for the predicate distinguishing countable from uncountable vertex sets.

title: Paths in Graphs
content: Defines a path as a list of vertices where consecutive entries are adjacent. This concrete representation (rather than Mathlib's `Walk` type) allows direct reasoning about internal vertices via list operations, which is essential for defining internal disjointness.
mathContext: A path $p = (v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_k)$ satisfies $v_i \sim v_{i+1}$ for all $0 \leq i < k$. The internal vertices are $\{v_1, \ldots, v_{k-1}\}$.

title: Internal Disjointness of Paths
content: Two paths are internally disjoint if they share no internal vertices (vertices that are neither first nor last). A collection of paths is pairwise internally disjoint if every pair is internally disjoint. This is the key concept for Menger's theorem: $k$-connectivity is equivalent to $k$ pairwise internally disjoint paths between any two vertices.
mathContext: Paths $p_1, p_2$ from $u$ to $v$ are internally disjoint iff $\text{int}(p_1) \cap \text{int}(p_2) = \emptyset$ where $\text{int}(p) = p \setminus \{u, v\}$. By Menger's theorem (1927), $\kappa(u,v) = $ max number of pairwise internally disjoint $u$-$v$ paths.

title: Infinite Vertex-Connectivity: InfinitelyManyDisjointPaths and InfinitelyConnected
content: `InfinitelyManyDisjointPaths G u v` asserts the existence of an infinite pairwise internally disjoint set of paths from u to v — the definition is existential over `Set (PathInGraph G)`, requiring the set to be infinite, pairwise internally disjoint, and all members to run from u to v. `InfinitelyConnected G` then requires this for all pairs of distinct vertices. This is an extremely strong property: by the infinite Menger theorem (Aharoni-Berger, 2009), it is equivalent to having no finite vertex cut separating any two vertices.
mathContext:
$$G \text{ is } \infty\text{-connected} \iff \forall u \neq v,\; \exists \text{ infinite set } \mathcal{P} \text{ of pairwise internally disjoint } u\text{-}v \text{ paths}$$
By the infinite Menger theorem (Aharoni-Berger 2009, *Inventiones Mathematicae*): $\kappa(u,v) = \aleph_0$ for all $u \neq v$, equivalently no finite vertex cut separates any two vertices.

title: Chromatic Number ≥ ℵ₁
content: Defines $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ via the negation of countable colorability: no function $c : V \to C$ with $C$ countable can be a proper coloring. By the De Bruijn-Erdős theorem (1951), this implies finite subgraphs with arbitrarily large chromatic number.
mathContext:
$$\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1 \iff \forall C \text{ countable},\; \forall c : V \to C,\; \exists u \sim v : c(u) = c(v)$$
By De Bruijn-Erdős, $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ implies $\chi(G) \geq k$ for every finite $k$.

title: Induced Subgraph on a Vertex Set
content: Constructs the induced subgraph $G[S]$ on a vertex set $S$: vertices are elements of $S$, edges are inherited from $G$. The `SimpleGraph` axioms (symmetry, no loops) are verified by delegating to $G$. This is the key construction for Problem 1068: we seek a countable $S$ such that $G[S]$ is infinitely connected.
mathContext: $G[S]$ has vertex set $S$ and edge set $\{(u,v) : u, v \in S,\, u \sim_G v\}$. The problem asks: $\exists S \subseteq V$ countable such that $G[S]$ is $\infty$-connected.

title: Erdős Problem 1068: The Main Conjecture
content: The central open question: does every graph with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ contain a countable vertex set $S$ such that $G[S]$ is infinitely connected? This is a weakening of Problem 1067 (disproved by Soukup). The restriction to countable subgraphs makes this fundamentally different — Soukup's counterexample controls uncountable sets but says nothing about countable ones.
mathContext: $$\forall G \text{ with } \chi(G) \geq \aleph_1,\; \exists S \subseteq V(G) : |S| \leq \aleph_0 \wedge G[S] \text{ is } \infty\text{-connected}$$

title: Soukup's Counterexample (2015)
content: Soukup (2015, *Combinatorica*) constructed in ZFC a graph with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ where every uncountable vertex set induces a graph that is NOT infinitely connected. The construction uses ladder systems on non-special trees: pairs of vertices from any uncountable set can be separated by a finite vertex cut. This makes the countable case (Problem 1068) the remaining open question.
mathContext:
$$\exists G : \chi(G) \geq \aleph_1 \wedge \forall S \subseteq V(G),\; |S| > \aleph_0 \implies G[S] \text{ is NOT } \infty\text{-connected}$$
Soukup's graph uses $\omega_1$-trees with ladder systems defining edges.

title: Problem 1067 Disproved
content: Problem 1067 asked whether every graph with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$ contains an infinitely connected subgraph with $\chi \geq \aleph_1$. Soukup showed the answer is NO. Problem 1068 weakens this by dropping the chromatic number requirement and only asking for countability of the subgraph.
mathContext:
Problem 1067 (DISPROVED): $\forall G$ with $\chi(G) \geq \aleph_1$, $\exists H \subseteq G$ with $H$ $\infty$-connected and $\chi(H) \geq \aleph_1$.
Problem 1068 (OPEN): replace $\chi(H) \geq \aleph_1$ with $|V(H)| \leq \aleph_0$.

title: No Finite Vertex Separator: Proof via Pigeonhole on Internally Disjoint Paths
content: `inf_connected_no_finite_separator` proves that in an infinitely connected graph, removing any finite set S of vertices still allows a path between any two non-S vertices. The proof uses a pigeonhole argument: define 'bad' paths as those with an internal vertex in S. By pairwise internal disjointness, each vertex of S is internal to at most ONE path (subsingleton fiber), so the set of bad paths is finite (bounded by |S|). Since infinitely many paths exist but only finitely many are bad, some 'good' path avoids S. The endpoint argument (lines 167-188) then shows vertices of p not in the interior must be endpoints u or v — if the head or last vertex of p is in S, that contradicts u ∉ S or v ∉ S.
mathContext: If $G$ is $\infty$-connected with paths $\mathcal{P}$ between $u,v$, and $S$ is finite with $u,v \notin S$: $\text{bad} = \{p \in \mathcal{P} : \exists s \in S, s \in \text{int}(p)\}$. Pairwise internal disjointness gives $|\text{bad}| \leq |S|$, so $\mathcal{P} \setminus \text{bad} \neq \emptyset$. In Lean: `Set.Finite.biUnion` with `Set.Subsingleton.finite` for the fiber bound.

title: Set-Theoretic Sensitivity and Bowler-Pikhurko Simplification
content: Lines 189-203 contain two docstring-only theorems (axiomatized as `True`). `set_theoretic_sensitivity` notes that Komjáth (2013, *Israel J. Math.*) showed a related question is independent of ZFC — the problem may also be sensitive to set-theoretic axioms beyond ZFC. `bowler_pikhurko_simplified_construction` records that Bowler and Pitz (2024, *Electronic J. Combinatorics*) simplified Soukup's counterexample for Problem #1067 using tree-like 'ladder' graphs (arXiv:2402.05984), though this doesn't resolve Problem #1068.
mathContext: Komjáth's independence result: a related question (#1067 with $\aleph_1$ vertices) is ZFC-independent via forcing. For Problem 1068, independence has not been established. Bowler-Pitz 2024: elementary ladder-graph construction replacing Soukup's non-special tree approach, preserving the key finite-vertex-cut property for uncountable sets.

title: Part VII: Proved Structural Implications and Summary
content: Part VII contains three fully proved theorems (no sorries, no axioms) establishing structural consequences of infinite connectivity. `inf_connected_implies_path` (lines 211-216): an infinitely connected graph is connected — extract one path from the infinite family. `inf_connected_subgraph_has_paths` (lines 218-225): if G[S] is infinitely connected, then any two vertices of S are path-connected within S. `inf_connected_k_connected` (lines 227-238): infinitely connected graphs are k-vertex-connected for every finite k — follows directly from `inf_connected_no_finite_separator` since no finite set S with |S| ≤ k blocks a path. The summary (lines 240-264) recaps the open status, Soukup's result, and the difficulty at the intersection of infinite combinatorics and set theory.
mathContext: $G$ $\infty$-connected $\Rightarrow$ $G$ is $k$-vertex-connected for all finite $k$: $\forall u \neq v$, $\forall S$ finite with $|S| \leq k$, $u,v \notin S$, $\exists u$-$v$ path avoiding $S$. The three proved theorems form a chain: $\infty$-connected $\Rightarrow$ path-connected $\Rightarrow$ $k$-connected for all $k$.
